planting.note: Start dormant tubers in warm, humid, bright shade in spring; this short-day species sets buds as autumn daylength shortens and flowers through winter indoors or in a frost-free greenhouse.

directions: Begonia socotrana is a tuberous species found only on the isolated island of Socotra off the Horn of Africa, where it grows tucked into shaded limestone crevices. It is best known not for garden display but for its role as a parent of the winter-flowering Lorraine and Hiemalis begonia hybrid groups, contributing its short-day blooming response and rounded, glossy leaves. Grow it in bright, indirect shade with high humidity and a free-draining mix, watering moderately while in active growth and letting it rest nearly dry once the tuber goes dormant after flowering. It is strictly a frost-free container or greenhouse plant outside the mildest climates.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in warm, humid, filtered shade in spring; this upright shrub-type begonia branches readily and benefits from pinching to stay bushy.

directions: Native to coastal forest understory in Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil, Begonia squamulosa is an upright, cane-like shrub species named for the small scale-like hairs that dust its stems and flower stalks. It bears loose clusters of small orange-red flowers over a long season and has been used by begonia breeders as a parent in developing compact flowering hybrids. Grow it in filtered shade with steady warmth and humidity, pinching young stems to encourage branching and discarding leggy old canes as new basal growth appears. It tolerates brief dry spells better than many fibrous-rooted begonias but still performs best with even moisture.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew)

planting.note: Divide rhizome sections in spring and grow on in warm, humid, bright shade; this East African montane species resents cold, soggy soil.

directions: Begonia meyeri-johannis is a rhizomatous species from montane forest understory in East Africa, including the lower slopes of the Kilimanjaro region, where it grows in deep leaf litter under a closed canopy. It forms clumps of large, softly hairy, heart-shaped leaves and produces clusters of pale pink to white flowers on arching stalks above the foliage. Provide warm, humid, bright shade and a loose, humus-rich mix that drains quickly, since the fleshy rhizomes rot readily in cold or waterlogged soil. It is primarily grown by begonia specialists as a houseplant or warm-greenhouse subject rather than as a mass-market bedding plant.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew)

planting.note: Divide small rhizome offsets in spring and grow in a closed terrarium or high-humidity case in bright shade; this miniature species dries out and browns quickly in open room air.

directions: Begonia bogneri is a diminutive rainforest-floor species from eastern Madagascar, unusual among begonias for its narrow, grass-like leaves instead of the broad rounded or lobed leaves typical of the genus. It forms a dense, tufted miniature rosette only a few inches across and sends up tiny flower stalks well above the foliage. Because its thin leaves lose moisture quickly, it is almost always grown under glass or in a closed terrarium with constant high humidity rather than in open room conditions. Use a light, fast-draining mix and keep it out of direct sun, which scorches the delicate foliage within hours.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew)

planting.note: Divide rhizome sections in spring and establish in warm, humid, bright shade; keep the thick rhizomes just above a free-draining mix rather than buried.

directions: Begonia antongilensis takes its name from the Antongil Bay region of northeastern Madagascar, where it grows as a low rhizomatous understory plant in humid rainforest. Its rounded leaves carry a distinctive bronze to coppery-red metallic sheen set off by darker contrasting veins, making it a foliage plant prized by begonia collectors more than a flowering specimen. Grow it in warm, bright shade with constant humidity and a loose, humus-rich, fast-draining mix, since the surface rhizomes are prone to rot if kept wet or buried too deep. It suits a humid windowsill, closed case, or warm greenhouse bench rather than open garden exposure outside the tropics.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew)
